column2: Acute MR (papillary rupture) into a small non-compliant LA gives a high wedge pressure with giant v waves. A saturation step-up in the RV suggests VSD.
Most sudden cardiac deaths occur in people without known heart disease or with EF > 35%; CAD underlies ~80% of adult cases.
Raised JVP with giant v waves, pulsatile liver and a pansystolic murmur at the lower left sternal edge (louder on inspiration) is tricuspid regurgitation.
Bilateral ankle oedema with normal JVP and investigations in a treated hypertensive is amlodipine oedema (arteriolar dilatation); it responds poorly to diuretics.
COPD with hypercapnia (flap), raised JVP and oedema is cor pulmonale: right heart failure from hypoxic pulmonary hypertension.
Raised JVP, pericardial knock (early S3), hepatomegaly and ascites out of proportion to oedema with a small pulse is constrictive pericarditis.
Rheumatic disease with an apical pansystolic murmur to the axilla, soft S1 and loud S3 is severe MR, with secondary right heart failure.
Fever, rigors and pleuritic pain with dullness, bronchial breathing and crackles over one zone is lobar pneumonia; assess with CURB-65 and CXR.
Sudden pleuritic pain in a tall young smoker with reduced expansion, hyper-resonance and reduced breath sounds is a primary spontaneous pneumothorax.
Swinging fever despite antibiotics with dullness and absent breath sounds at the base is empyema; aspirate (pH < 7.2, pus) and insert a chest drain.
Sharp central pain to the shoulder, fever and a friction rub is acute pericarditis (saddle ST elevation, PR depression); NSAID plus colchicine.
Exertional pain in a young man with a double apical impulse and ejection systolic murmur is HOCM; louder with Valsalva, confirm by echo.
Arm hypertension with lower leg pressures and an ejection click (bicuspid valve) in a young adult is coarctation; confirm by CT/MR angiography.
Exertional symptoms with a jerky pulse, double apical impulse and ejection murmur are HOCM; aortic stenosis gives a slow-rising pulse.
Hypotension, pulsus paradoxus, grossly raised JVP and soft heart sounds in lung cancer is malignant tamponade: urgent pericardiocentesis.
Cardiogenic shock with a markedly raised troponin a week after a viral illness is fulminant myocarditis; support, and recovery is often good.
Raised JVP, pericardial knock, hepatomegaly, ascites and oedema is chronic constrictive pericarditis; tamponade is acute with soft heart sounds.
Unilateral painful leg swelling on the pill after long-haul travel is DVT: Wells score, D-dimer/ultrasound, then a DOAC.
Long-standing COPD with a flap, raised JVP and oedema is cor pulmonale; LTOT improves survival in eligible patients.
Hot, red, tender swollen leg with raised WCC and normal Doppler is cellulitis; treat with flucloxacillin (doxycycline/clarithromycin if allergic).
Ascites and hepatomegaly out of proportion to oedema, raised JVP and pericardial knock indicate constrictive pericarditis; pericardiectomy is definitive.
Progressive breathlessness with raised JVP, oedema and bibasal crackles in poorly treated IHD is congestive heart failure; NT-proBNP and echo.
Hypertension with hypokalaemia and alkalosis in a young woman suggests Conn's syndrome; screen with the aldosterone:renin ratio.
Paroxysmal palpitations and chest pain with raised urinary catecholamines is phaeochromocytoma; alpha-block before any beta-blocker.
Weight gain, proximal weakness, hirsutism, oedema and hypertension suggest Cushing's syndrome; screen with overnight dexamethasone suppression.
BP 220/145 with papilloedema and retinal haemorrhages is malignant hypertension; lower by ≤ 25% in the first hours with IV labetalol or nitroprusside.
New hypertension in an elderly smoker with widespread atherosclerosis suggests atheromatous renal artery stenosis; confirm with duplex or CT/MR angiography.
Sudden tearing pain to the back in a hypertensive man is aortic dissection; confirm with CT angiography and never thrombolyse.
Sudden breathlessness and tachycardia after hip replacement with right axis deviation (RV strain) is PE; CTPA and anticoagulate.
Exertional crushing pain relieved by rest with a normal ECG afterwards is stable angina; CT coronary angiography is the first test.
Pleuritic pain and breathlessness in a tall young athlete with hyper-resonance on one side is spontaneous pneumothorax.
Localised chest-wall pain reproduced by light pressure and relieved by NSAIDs, with a normal ECG, is costochondritis.
Before elective cardioversion of AF > 48 h: ≥ 3 weeks of anticoagulation (DOAC now preferred) with rate control (digoxin in HFrEF), continued ≥ 4 weeks after.
Recurrent VT in acute MI despite beta-blocker and electrolyte correction: IV amiodarone; lidocaine is a second-line IV alternative.
IV adenosine transiently blocks the AV node: it terminates AVNRT/AVRT and unmasks flutter, so it is diagnostic and therapeutic. Avoid in severe asthma.
Torsades de pointes: IV magnesium 2 g, correct K⁺, stop QT drugs, and overdrive pacing or isoprenaline to prevent recurrence. Amiodarone is contraindicated.
A tapping apex with a low-pitched apical mid-diastolic rumble is mitral stenosis, almost always rheumatic.
Fixed wide S2 splitting with a pulmonary flow murmur is ASD; the ECG shows RBBB.
Loud P2 with raised JVP, hepatic congestion and functional TR indicates pulmonary hypertension with right heart failure.
Slow-rising small-volume pulse, heaving apex and ejection murmur to the carotids is aortic stenosis; symptoms mean valve replacement.
Arm hypertension with a systolic murmur between the scapulae is coarctation; check radiofemoral delay and rib notching.
Aching legs after standing with haemosiderin pigmentation at the ankles is chronic venous insufficiency; compression once ABPI is normal.
Sudden severe limb pain with an irregular pulse (AF) is embolic acute limb ischaemia: IV heparin and urgent embolectomy.
Cyanotic spells, squatting and an ejection systolic murmur in a toddler is tetralogy of Fallot.
Fixed S2 splitting with a pulmonary flow murmur in a young adult is ASD; echo confirms and significant defects are closed by device.
